doc.title: Larry Ridley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 10, 2003

title: Monk Montgomery hands him the bass; Wes and the Montgomery-Johnson Quintet
summary: Monk Montgomery had him fill in at the Turf Club while he went west; Ridley learned by listening to Wes and the group, and he also lists his violin teachers.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: No Conte Candoli, that was something —
I’m sorry, I missed what you said.

The group with Freddie Hubbard and Jimmy Spaulding and first Walt Miller then Al Plank and Paul Parker was the drummer. And then we used to play with Wes. The first time I saw Monk Montgomery and I approached him about taking lessons from him he told me, “Well come over to the house, kid.” I went over to the house and there is Wes sitting up there with the guitar and his brother Buddy at the piano. A saxophone player by the name of Pookie Johnson and the drummer Sonny Johnson. They called themselves the Montgomery-Johnson Quintet and they had a steady gig working in a place called the Turf Club. So Monk says, “Go over and pick up the bass.” I said, “What?” “Go over and pick up the bass.” So I went over and picked up the bass and they struck up a tune. And I’m saying wait a minute, what’s happening here. He said, “Look kid, I’m going out to the west coast because I’m beginning, starting a group called The Master Sounds, and I’m going to have to go out there to set up some business and I’m going to be gone for two weeks and I want you to fill in for me.” “Yes sir, Mister Montgomery.” And here I was man, that was his way of teaching me. He never really gave me a lesson other than me absorbing and listening and watching and listening to him perform. But as far as saying okay you do this and you do that, I taught myself that in the very beginning. And of course I knew from playing the violin you know, so I taught myself the bass clef and all that. And then I had great teachers on the violin. I had a young lady who was with the Indianapolis Symphony Orchestra who was my teacher. There was a woman by the name of Ruth MacArthur who had a conservatory there. She was a young African-American woman who set up a conservatory, and Slide Hampton and his whole family and all of us used to go there. And she had a relationship with the Indianapolis Symphony Orchestra where she got some of the players to teach us, in the African-American community. And they would come in and give us lessons. And so we had excellent training. And then there was some gentlemen there who were excellent mentors who taught, Mr. Russell Brown, Mr. James Compton and Laverne Newsom who taught at the high school and also in the elementary schools, Mr. Lawrence Leggett who taught me in the third grade when I was in my little elementary school orchestra. And so we had excellent instruction. And the thing was learning about it, and what I learned from Wes, it was so important, that I tried to reflect to my students how important, part of playing jazz and playing music period is © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-
